caption:
Three days after he quit as Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang has talked with confidants about coming back, the Financial Times reports.
An ally says a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives is forming to lobby for his return. Huang has no controlling stake, so the board decides.

Should Nvidia take him back?

site_article.summary: Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12, 2026, has talked with confidants about a possible return, according to the Financial Times. An ally said a group of Silicon Valley executives is forming to lobby the board for his reinstatement.
site_article.seo_title: Jensen Huang weighs a return to Nvidia, FT reports
site_article.seo_description: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has discussed coming back, the Financial Times reports, as allies lobby the board and Bessent calls for a shakeup.
site_article.answer_summary: According to the Financial Times, Jensen Huang has privately discussed returning as Nvidia's chief executive, but neither he nor Nvidia has confirmed it, and only the board can reinstate him.

paragraphs.text: Jensen Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning as chief executive of Nvidia, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, November 15, 2026, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang stepped down as chief executive on November 12. Spokespeople for Nvidia and for Huang declined to comment to the newspaper, and Fortune noted that the report has not been confirmed by either.

According to the report, an ally of Huang said a group of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled as a "war room" to lobby for his reinstatement and to seek support from the White House. The same ally said Huang supported those efforts and described his standing in the industry by saying that everyone who matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves him.

Huang resigned after reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and with a subordinate, The Jerusalem Post wrote in its account of the Financial Times story. Those reports have not been confirmed, and an independent board investigation into his conduct is continuing. Another person involved in the push for his return acknowledged that an affair with a subordinate is grounds for dismissal.

The reported relationship involved Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed. Citing The Information, Fortune reported that Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years. Megaspeed has said it conducts lawful business, has hired outside counsel for an internal investigation, and that Alice Huang left the company effective August 30, 2025.

Elon Musk has argued publicly for Huang's return. In posts on X on November 14, Musk wrote that without Huang at least some critical deals would be lost, and said many supply agreements had been a handshake with Huang rather than a written contract. He did not say how many deals were at risk. An open letter calling for Huang to be brought back gained support over the weekend from Musk, Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney and several Nvidia employees.

Nvidia shareholders Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management wrote to the board on Friday, November 13, urging it to keep a possible return on the table, citing his record and the uncertainty around his departure.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took the opposite view on Fox News on November 15. He said the board should look outside the company for a new chief executive and needed a dramatic shakeup, and said that if Nvidia were a bank that had not complied with export rules, regulators would already be involved and many executives would be removed. He called Nvidia a wonderful company and Huang an incredible innovator, but said that did not excuse compliance failures.

Huang does not hold a controlling stake and cannot override the board, according to the report. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and Harvey Jones became Nvidia's first board chair on November 12. The Financial Times reported on Friday that the board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor, while the board said no formal process had begun. Fortune listed Kress and senior engineer Ian Buck as possible internal candidates and Haas and AMD chief executive Lisa Su as outside names, without a confirmed shortlist.

Markets were closed when the report appeared. Nvidia shares closed at $162.85 on November 13, down 26.41 percent over the past month, according to 24/7 Wall St. The company reports quarterly results on Tuesday, November 17.

The report sets up a direct contest between Huang's allies in the industry and a board under pressure from Washington to show it takes export compliance seriously. A return would ease concerns about informal supply relationships that Musk described, but it would cut against the ongoing conduct investigation and the administration's public demand for outside leadership.

The earnings call on November 17 is the first moment Nvidia's interim leadership will face analysts, and any comment on the succession search or the board investigation will signal whether a Huang return is realistic.
